rv.q: It's a broken, brilliant Seagull – and it flies.
But if you're open to a show that makes noise quietly and thinks deeply, this 'Seagull' really flies.

In one of the most revelatory productions of the past decade he, and translator Martin Crimp, turned Cyrano de Bergerac from a big-nose-and-boots-boys flamboyant indulgence into something immediate and rasping.
Fortunately, those performances are uniformly gripping, the character's clashing complications gelling together in a messy but compellingly believable whole.

Prior to the pandemic, Jamie Lloyd, puckish purveyor of “event theatre”, gave us one of the most arresting productions of recent times with a stripped-back, casually dressed Cyrano de Bergerac starring James McAvoy that featured, near scandalously, no “nose”.
I found it unrewarding: slow-burning, always undercutting itself, to little end.
Yes, you feel trapped, suffocated by Lloyd's pretentiousness.
Lloyd's The Seagull is a most unusual interpretation, but it works, making the play feel more relevant than I can remember from previous productions.
Reiss's telling hits the human spirit with great exactitude.

If you are willing to listen carefully enough, this play whispers many of its secrets to you within the first few minutes, which comes as little surprise from the playwright whose name has become synonymous with theatrical foreshadowing.
Fresh though this initially seems, the chairs and largely seated actors most strongly evoke the practice of the legendary dance-theatre maker Pina Bausch (who died 13 years ago).

This is a stylish, distinctive production. However, its narrative arc abandons character complexity or development as it moves from one character's despair to suicide in a context of unremitting gloom.
The director's eccentric minimalism isn't just banal and unoriginal. It's an affront to theatre lovers.
Some may miss the accoutrements of a lavish staging but I loved seeing the actors' craft as they inhabit their characters, using only voice and their bodies.
It is skilfully done but at times it does feel a bit interminable.
